messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 26
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Fisherman
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 37

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory (Babies): Babies, Public Transport: Bus riding, Feeling Vulnerable: Feeling emotionally vulnerable
  Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
  Memory: Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Clinical Vignette: Marcus

Marcus was twenty-three when the men came for him. He had been working a fishing boat out of a small harbor in Maine, a job he'd held for three years without incident—honest work that kept him on the water and away from the small-town entanglements his older brother had fallen into. One evening in late autumn, after he'd tied off the boat and was walking to his truck, a van pulled alongside him. He remembered the sound of the sliding door, the hands that grabbed his jacket, the sensation of being pulled into darkness. What followed over the next eight hours was a calculated destruction of his sense of safety. His captors—men he later learned were connected to a debt his brother owed—had restrained him against a concrete wall in a basement, his back pressed hard against the cold surface while they took turns questioning him about money he didn't have. They had used implements from the room itself as threats: a rusted metal pipe, a length of chain, broken glass arranged deliberately where he could see it. The pain was methodical rather than frenzied, designed to break him rather than kill him. When his brother finally paid what was owed, they released him with a warning never to speak about what had happened.

Three years have passed since that night. Marcus is now twenty-six, married to Elena for fourteen months, and he has come to see the world as a place organized around threat. He can no longer work the fishing boat. The first time he tried to return, three weeks after his release, he lasted forty minutes before the rocking motion and the enclosed cabin triggered a panic so severe he thought his heart would stop. More insidious than that acute reaction was the slow erosion of his ability to be anywhere without calculating angles and exits. He has come to believe that safety exists only when his back is against something solid and he can see the entire room—a requirement that has made ordinary life nearly impossible. At restaurants, he positions himself in corners. On the rare occasions Elena convinces him to ride the bus with her to visit her family, he sits at the back, his shoulders rigid, his eyes fixed on the driver and the other passengers. What terrifies him most is not the memory itself but the certainty that danger is always present, always watching, always looking for the moment when he is exposed.

The auditory world has become a minefield. When a baby cries in the grocery store—a sound Elena finds merely annoying—Marcus's body goes rigid. The pitch and helplessness in that sound triggers something primal in him, a reminder of vulnerability, of being unable to escape or control what is happening. He has stopped going to the store with her. He listens constantly for sounds that might mean someone is entering their apartment, and he has installed three new locks on the door, each one a small ritual of reassurance that never quite reassures. When they are anywhere public, his attention narrows to potential weapons: the heavy candlestick on the restaurant table, the rake leaning against a neighbor's shed, the way a man's hands move when he reaches into his jacket. Elena has noticed that he sees danger where none exists, but she does not yet understand that his vigilance is not paranoia—it is the only thing standing between him and a return to that basement.

The memories themselves come without warning and with a physicality that is difficult to describe to anyone who has not experienced it. When the image of his back against that wall surfaces—often at night, sometimes triggered by nothing he can identify—his body positions itself exactly as it was then, muscles contracting into that same posture of helpless resistance. The pain returns too, not imagined but felt, a sharp ache across his lower back and shoulders, as if the memory has somehow reanimated the nerve endings themselves. When this happens, a rage unlike anything he has ever known rises up in him, a fury so consuming that he has to leave the bedroom so he does not frighten Elena. He has punched walls twice. He has not told her about the rage, only that he needs to walk.

What brought him to seek help now was Elena's ultimatum, delivered gently but firmly: she loves him, but she cannot stay married to someone who is disappearing. She is right. He knows he is disappearing. He came to his first appointment with a therapist last week, and what he most wants to know is whether it is possible to ever feel safe again, or whether the basement has followed him out into the world and will never let him go.
